title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(L\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.
why: Many applications need an assignment rather than recognition that an assignment must exist. A universal implication would connect tractability classifications of promise decision problems to actual construction across finite local constraint languages. A separation would identify a fixed finite promise problem whose decision gap is efficiently recognizable while its promised solutions resist every deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm.

importance.reason: A foundational search-versus-decision question spanning graph colouring, satisfiability and the algebraic classification of finite PCSPs.

progress.text: The algebraic framework and survey distinguish finite-template decision from search and describe constructive special cases.
The robust-satisfiability paper establishes new constructive guarantees for Boolean majority-preserved templates and related larger-domain classes, under explicit structural hypotheses.
Larrauri’s v4 proves hardness for rounding relaxation-accepted inputs and undecidability of template meta-problems, but §10 explicitly retains the original per-template tractability implication.

status_note: The fixed-template question is explicitly open in §10 pp. 59–60 of Larrauri v4, 25 May 2026. Its relaxation-accepted rounding hardness and varying-template undecidability do not settle the promised search problem. A bounded primary-source search and revision check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The February 2026 robust-satisfiability results apply under additional preservation hypotheses; cited proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: The strong template A describes the constraints guaranteed to be simultaneously satisfiable; B describes the weaker constraints an answer must satisfy. The map from A to B proves that a weak answer exists whenever a strong one exists, but the input supplies only that existence promise. A decision algorithm recognizes the promised gap, whereas search must actually construct the weaker assignment.

For graph colouring, one may take A and B to be complete graphs on three and six vertices. Search then asks for a six-colouring of a graph promised to admit a three-colouring. Decision only separates three-colourable graphs from graphs admitting no six-colouring; it has no required behaviour on graphs with chromatic number four, five or six. This example illustrates the promise and does not assert tractability for that particular pair.

A polynomial-time search algorithm implies decision by returning a proposed weak assignment that can be checked. The reverse implication is known for ordinary fixed finite CSPs, where A=B. With two templates, fixing a variable to a weak-domain value can destroy the stronger promise, so ordinary decision self-reducibility does not automatically apply.

Known constructive cases include templates admitting a fixed finite intermediate structure C with A→C→B and tractable CSP(C). The survey also discusses tractable promise problems whose explanation requires more than such a finite intermediate problem, under the usual separation assumptions. Thus the ordinary CSP case does not supply the general statement.

Larrauri studies rounding for three standard decision relaxations: the basic linear program using consistent local distributions, an affine integer program, and their combination. Finding a weak assignment on every input accepted by one of these relaxations can encode arbitrary total NP search problems. A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.

sentences: A finite promise CSP distinguishes strong constraints whose satisfiability is guaranteed from weaker constraints an output must satisfy.
The decision problem separates strongly satisfiable inputs from those with no weak solution.
The question asks whether every fixed template with a deterministic polynomial-time decider also permits deterministic polynomial-time construction on the original stronger promise.
Hardness of rounding arbitrary relaxation-accepted inputs and undecidability of template recognition leave this implication unresolved.
A resolution would clarify whether tractability of finite promise constraints always extends from recognizing feasibility to producing assignments.
